subject: physics
question_text: Pendulum clocks generally go fast in winter and slow in summer. Why?

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2017 (Q18), March 2019 (Q18) and March 2023 (Q18) — Section B, 4 marks each time. Sourced from those papers (answer-book/papers/), not from either guide book, which is why the manifest entry carries source "ts_paper" and stars 0. The four-way split is invented and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: T = 2π√(L/g); L = L₀(1 + αΔθ); differentiating gives ΔT/T = ½ ΔL/L = ½ αΔθ.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The period depends on the length
lines: A pendulum clock measures time by counting
the swings of its pendulum. For a simple
so only L and g set the period.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the formula before saying anything about hot or cold.
steps.why: The whole answer follows from T rising when L rises. The mass of the bob is not in the formula, so a change of season can act only through L.
common_mistakes: Saying the mass of the bob changes with temperature — the mass never enters T = 2π√(L/g).

recall.must_convey: That the clock counts swings and the period is T = 2π root L by g.
accept: T is 2 pi root L by g

steps.memory_tip: Only L and g sit in T = 2π√(L/g). Temperature can reach the clock only through L.

steps.label: The rod expands and contracts
lines: The pendulum rod is metal. It gets longer
when heated and shorter when cooled:
α is the coefficient of linear expansion
of the rod and Δθ is the change in
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the ROD as the part that changes length.
steps.why: This is the only place temperature enters the problem. A pendulum with a rod that did not expand would keep the same time in every season.
common_mistakes: Reading Δθ as the temperature itself. It is the CHANGE in temperature.

recall.must_convey: That the metal rod expands on heating, L = L naught into one plus alpha delta theta.
accept: L naught into one plus alpha delta theta
reject: T is 2 pi root L by g

steps.memory_tip: Metal rod, hotter, longer. The season acts on the rod, never on the bob.

steps.label: Summer — the clock runs slow
lines: In summer Δθ is positive, so L increases.
A larger L gives a larger T, so each swing
takes longer and fewer swings are completed

lines.text: L ↑ ⇒ T ↑ ⇒ the clock runs SLOW

steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both halves are needed: L increases, therefore T increases.
steps.why: A pendulum clock displays the number of swings it has counted. Longer swings mean fewer counted in a real day, so the display reads less than the true time.
common_mistakes: Saying a longer pendulum swings faster. A longer pendulum swings SLOWER.

recall.must_convey: That in summer L increases, T increases, and the clock runs slow.

steps.memory_tip: Longer pendulum, longer swing, fewer swings counted. Summer clock is slow.

steps.label: Winter — the clock runs fast
lines: In winter Δθ is negative, so L decreases.
A smaller L gives a smaller T, and more
swings are completed in one real day.
The fractional change follows from the
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The ½ that the square root puts there is what is checked.
steps.why: The period goes as the square root of the length, so a 1% rise in L changes T by only about 0.5%. That factor of one half is the whole reason the formula is not ΔT/T = αΔθ.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔT/T = αΔθ and dropping the ½ that the square root introduces.

recall.must_convey: That in winter L decreases, T decreases, the clock runs fast, and delta T by T is half alpha delta theta.

steps.memory_tip: The square root halves it: ΔT/T = ½ αΔθ, never αΔθ.

insider_note: Two of the four marks are the two seasons, so write both directions even when the question names only one. The ½ in ΔT/T = ½ αΔθ is the line most students drop.
